extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, scholars, and policymakers (those studying or litigating prior-user rights under the AIA)
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative-history and statutory explanation of the prior-user defense created/modified by the Leahy‑Smith America Invents Act (35 U.S.C. §273), describing the elements, limits, examples, and policy rationales for when a party is entitled to continue secret commercial use of subject matter that would otherwise infringe. Useful for attorneys, policy analysts, and courts construing §273.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement: Good-faith commercial use in the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: (a)(1) such person, acting in good faith, commercially used the subject matter in the United States, either in connection with an internal commercial use or an actual arm’s length sale or other arm’s length commercial transfer of a useful end result of such commercial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senator Leahy: the phrase 'commercially used the subject matter' is intended to apply broadly to any form of subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) used in a manufacturing or other commercial process. Internal commercial use qualifies if integrated into an ongoing commercial process and not merely fleeting, experimental, or incidental (e.g., customized internal software used continuously).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: One-year pre-filing or pre-disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: (a)(2) such commercial use occurred at least 1 year before the earlier of either (A) the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or (B) the date on which the claimed invention was disclosed to the public in a manner that qualified for the exception from prior art under section 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-year gap was part of the House compromise with universities; it helps ensure the prior user did not derive the invention from the patentee and that the prior user was the earlier party to invent (assuming reasonable diligence by patentee). Critics argued the one-year limit can deny rights to clear first inventors; some earlier proposals required shorter gaps or reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter limitation: process or items used in a manufacturing/other commercial process
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(a) limits the prior-user defense to either a 'process' or to a machine, manufacture, or composition of matter used in a manufacturing or other commercial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction (similar to earlier AIPA language) effectively precludes assertion for ordinary consumer products that become public on sale; it covers tools, devices, or substances used inside a closed factory or exhausted in a manufacturing process, and thus permits defense for items that do not become prior art by public sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-result concept (subject matter vs useful end result)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (d) and (a)(1)/(d) use the concept of a 'useful end result' and imply the 'subject matter' protected by §273 is a process or tool used to make another product, not the final consumer product itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'end result' language implies prior-user protection attaches to processes/tools and their produced results; e.g., a product-by-process claim may allow extension to a finished consumer product, but normally final consumer products that are publicly sold become prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of rights when prior user sells useful end result
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(d): the sale or other disposition of a useful end result by a person entitled to assert a defense under this section ... shall exhaust the patent owner’s rights under the patent to the extent that such rights would have been exhausted had such sale or other disposition been made by the patent owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhaustion ensures purchasers from a prior user have the same resale/use rights as if they had bought from the patent owner (Quanta example). AIA added 'notwithstanding subsection (e)(1)' to clarify exhaustion supersedes the otherwise personal, nontransferable nature of the defense so customers are not left infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal commercial use must be continuous and integrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal commercial use qualifies when the use is integrated into an ongoing commercial process and is not merely fleeting, experimental, or incidental to the enterprise's operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senator Kyl example: customized software running a company's HR system qualifies. Senators agreed continuous internal use vests prior-user rights even for prototypes modified later; continuous use may qualify despite prototypes lacking commercial merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premarketing regulatory review deemed commercial use
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(c)(1): Subject matter for which commercial marketing or use is subject to a premarketing regulatory review period ... shall be deemed to be commercially used for purposes of subsection (a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treats time spent in regulatory review (e.g., FDA review) as commercial use for vesting prior-user rights (including any period specified in section 156(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprofit laboratory use deemed commercial use (limited to continued noncommercial lab use)
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(c)(2): Use by a nonprofit research laboratory or other nonprofit entity ... for which the public is the intended beneficiary, shall be deemed to be a commercial use for purposes of subsection (a)(1), except that a defense under this section may be asserted pursuant to this paragraph only for continued and noncommercial use by and in the laboratory or other nonprofit entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA consolidated earlier provisions treating certain nonprofit/university uses as commercial for vesting, but limited the defense to continued noncommercial use within the nonprofit laboratory or entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'substantial preparations' predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier proposals would have allowed vesting upon 'substantial preparations' to engage in commercial use; universities opposed this as vague and litigation-prone, so the final House agreement did not include a substantial-preparations predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history: substantial-preparations was considered vague and would weaken patent value; Congress left open possibility of revisiting issue later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the defense: legal (absolute) not equitable
rubrics_metrics.description: §273 creates an absolute legal defense to infringement, rather than an equitable defense that would allow courts to assess royalties against a defendant who successfully asserted the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory Commission had recommended equitable (royalty) approach; proponents of legal defense argued equitable valuation is difficult, would hinder alienability of businesses holding prior-user rights, and might discourage domestic manufacturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal defense: who may assert it (performer or director; affiliates allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(e)(1)(A): A defense under this section may be asserted only by the person who performed or directed the performance of the commercial use described in subsection (a), or by an entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with such person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA broadened access to affiliates (control/common control) but kept defense personal: only persons who performed or directed performance may assert it. This was modified from earlier drafts which used 'caused' (broader) to 'directed' (narrower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor/vendor use limited to 'directed' performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Change from allowing uses 'caused' by the defendant to allowing uses 'directed' by the defendant; 'directed' requires evidence the defendant affirmatively directed the vendor or contractor in the manner of the work or use of the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits third-party uses reaching back to the defendant: mere independent vendor use without instruction or contemporaneous knowledge does not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer/assignment restrictions (only with sale of entire enterprise/line of business)
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(e)(1)(B): Except for any transfer to the patent owner, the right to assert a defense under this section shall not be licensed or assigned or transferred to another person except as an ancillary and subordinate part of a good-faith assignment or transfer for other reasons of the entire enterprise or line of business to which the defense relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee example: defense tied to a specific piece of machinery cannot be transferred separately unless the entire commercial establishment is transferred. Restriction intended to prevent turning the personal right into a transferable compulsory-license-like authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on sites where a transferred defense may be used
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(e)(1)(C): When acquired as part of an assignment/transfer, the defense may only be asserted for uses at sites where the subject matter was in use before the later of the effective filing date or the date of assignment/transfer of such enterprise or line of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee Report: 'site' means a factory site or other major facility with significant capital investment and does not include offsite development locations or minor offsite manufacturing; this limits geographic/operational scope following transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation bar: no defense if subject matter derived from patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: §273(e)(2): A person may not assert a defense under this section if the subject matter on which the defense is based was derived from the patentee or persons in privity with the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents assertion where prior user misappropriated the invention or acquired knowledge illegitimately; reflects advisory commission recommendations and prior bill language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products sold to public generally become prior art (no PCU needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, products that are sold to consumers will not need a prior-commercial-use (PCU) defense over the long term because as soon as the product is sold to the public, any invention embodied in that product becomes prior art and cannot be patented by another party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist for products that never become accessible to the public (used only inside closed factories or exhausted in a manufacturing process), which §273 permits to be covered by the defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/replacement standards: reduction to practice vs commercial use
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier bills sometimes required reduction to practice at least one year before filing (or allowed substantial preparations); the enacted AIA requires commercial use at least one year before filing or public disclosure, expanding/altering earlier predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history describes how the requirement evolved: e.g., AIPA and 1995 bills differed; understanding the historical alternatives helps interpret scope and purpose of current §273 timing and subject-matter rules.
